title: Transfer: Redundant Connection
oneLiner: A tree got one extra edge. Find the edge to remove. Union-find again, watching for the one union whose two ends are already connected.
keyTakeaway: Add the edges one by one with union-find. An edge whose two ends already have the same root joins two nodes that are already connected, so it closes a cycle. A tree plus one edge has exactly one cycle, and the first such edge is the last of that cycle's edges in the input, which is the answer.
explanation:
This follows Union-Find: Count Connected Components with the question changed. A tree on n nodes, numbered 0 to n - 1, had one extra edge added between two different nodes, giving n edges in total. edges[i] = [a, b] is an undirected edge. Return an edge whose removal leaves a tree again; if several would work, return the one that appears last in edges.

In the parent lesson, an edge whose ends already shared a root changed nothing and was skipped. Here that edge is the whole point. If Find(a) == Find(b) before the union, a and b were already connected by edges seen earlier, so this edge plus that path forms a cycle. Return it.

Why is that the right one to return? Adding one edge to a tree creates exactly one cycle, and removing any edge on it restores a tree; edges off the cycle are needed. Processing in input order, union-find first reports a cycle at the moment its last edge arrives, since before then the cycle isn't closed. So the first redundant edge found is the cycle edge that appears last, which is the tie-break the problem asks for.

You don't need n as a parameter: a tree plus one edge has as many edges as nodes, so n is edges.Length. With path compression and union by size each operation is effectively O(1), so the pass is effectively O(n) time and O(n) space.

The visualization runs [[0, 1], [1, 2], [2, 3], [0, 3], [0, 4]] and shows the parent array.

Explain why the same idea works: before you move on, write two or three sentences comparing this with Count Connected Components. What does Find(a) == Find(b) mean in both problems, why is the first such edge also the last cycle edge in the input, and why does union-find suit edges arriving one at a time?

visualizationSteps.message: 5 edges, so 5 nodes. parent[i] = i: every node is its own root. Add the edges in order.
Edge [0, 1]: roots 0 and 1 differ, so the edge joins two separate groups. Union: parent[0] = 1.
Edge [1, 2]: roots 1 and 2 differ, so the edge joins two separate groups. Union: parent[1] = 2.
Edge [2, 3]: roots 2 and 3 differ, so the edge joins two separate groups. Union: parent[2] = 3.
Edge [0, 3]: Find(0) = Find(3) = 3. They are already connected, so this edge closes a cycle. Return [0, 3].

recognitionSignals: Edges arrive one at a time and you must spot the first one that connects two already connected nodes.
"A tree with one extra edge", "which connection creates a loop", or cycle detection in an undirected graph.
gotchas: Check Find(a) == Find(b) BEFORE the union; after it they always match.
Return the edge exactly as it appears in the input, in its original order [a, b].
There are as many nodes as edges here; size the parent array from edges.Length.
confusableWith: Union-Find: Count Connected Components counts the unions that merge two groups; this returns the one union that finds both ends already in one group.
Cycle Detection: Course Schedule finds cycles in a DIRECTED graph and needs the three colour DFS. In an undirected graph, union-find detects a cycle with no colours at all.

complexity.note: Here n is the number of edges, which is also the number of nodes. Each edge does two finds and at most one union; with path halving and union by size each is amortized α(n), effectively O(1). Space is the parent and size arrays.
